title: Java in the browser
lead: Java reaches this site in two ways. In the online mode, Java runs on a server, and the page calls it over the network through a client that Hilla generates. In the offline site, TeaVM compiles the Java search to WebAssembly or JavaScript, and the browser runs it in a Web Worker. This page follows one call along each path and shows what may cross each boundary.
toc.teavm: TeaVM: Java compiled for the browser
sec.overview.title: Two paths into the browser
sec.overview.p1: Java and JavaScript meet in two places in this project. In the online mode, a Spring Boot server runs Java engines, and the page calls them over HTTP. {term:hilla|Hilla} generates the TypeScript client for these calls, so no hand-written REST layer sits between page and server. In the offline site, no server code runs: {term:teavm|TeaVM} compiles the Java search ahead of time, and the browser runs the result in a {term:web-worker|Web Worker}, a background thread of the page.
sec.overview.p2: The two paths have different boundaries. On the Hilla path, page and JVM share no process and no memory, so every argument and every result crosses the network as JSON text. On the TeaVM path, the compiled Java runs in the browser, and TypeScript code calls it directly, as a function. What may cross that call depends on the build: JavaScript, {term:wasm-gc|Wasm GC}, or, for comparison, the C++ engine compiled to {term:wasm|WebAssembly}. The page itself talks to the worker only through messages.
sec.overview.p3: The offline site is a set of static files and needs no server ({sec:architecture/offline|offline architecture}). The online mode adds the server engines and keeps the browser engines. If the server does not answer, the page offers only the browser engines ({src:web/src/engines/server/load.ts}).
sec.hilla.title: Hilla: Java on the server
sec.hilla.p1: In the online mode, one Java class carries `@BrowserCallable` and `@AnonymousAllowed`. The first annotation makes it a {term:browser-callable|browser-callable service}; the second lets callers use it without a login, because Hilla denies every call by default. The class is a normal Spring bean with constructor injection and three public methods: `engines`, `legalMoves` and `choose` ({src:app/src/main/java/sternhalma/app/GameEndpoint.java}). During the build, {term:hilla|Hilla} 25.3.5 generates a TypeScript function for each method and a TypeScript interface for each Java record that a method returns, such as `ServerChoice`. The generated files are build products and are not in Git.
sec.hilla.p2: The generated function looks like a local async function, but it is a stand-in. JavaScript cannot call the Java method directly: the method runs in the JVM of the server process, the page runs in the browser, and the two share no memory. HTTP is the only link. Each call is a `POST /connect/GameEndpoint/<method>` with the parameters as one JSON object. Hilla's client adds the {term:csrf-token|CSRF token} in the header `X-CSRF-Token`, and the server checks it in each call. The answer is the record as JSON, so the page receives a copy; the Java object stays on the server.
sec.hilla.p3: On the page, the TypeScript adapter of the server engines loads the generated client with a dynamic import and passes it on as a small interface. So the adapter knows nothing about Hilla, and its tests run without it ({src:web/src/engines/server/load.ts}). In the offline build, Vite drops this import, and the build script fails if a bundled script contains a `connect/` path. On the server, every call is stateless: the engine replays the move history from the start position. A semaphore limits the concurrent searches to the number of cores, and a call that asks for more than {n:5000000} nodes is rejected ({src:app/src/main/java/sternhalma/app/Engines.java}).
sec.hilla.p4: The limits, as the code shows them: the server engines play only the default variant, adjacent jumps with two players, and have no analysis. The endpoint allows anonymous calls, so the start script binds the app to `127.0.0.1` by default. The jar copies the engine and table files of the web app but not the network models ({src:app/build.gradle.kts}). The net engines in the browser therefore probably lack their models in the online build; this follows from the build script and was not tried. CI does not run the Hilla production build.
sec.teavm.title: TeaVM: Java compiled for the browser
sec.teavm.p1: {term:teavm|TeaVM} describes itself as an ahead-of-time compiler of Java bytecode to JavaScript. Its input is the class files that javac writes, not the Java source, so it is a compiler rather than a {term:transpiler|transpiler} in the strict sense. TeaVM 0.16.0 builds two targets from the same Java code: an ES2015 module in JavaScript and a {term:wasm-gc|Wasm GC} module, WebAssembly with garbage collection ({src:teavm-web/build.gradle.kts}). The Wasm GC build `java-wasmgc` is the default engine of this site. A browser without Wasm GC gets the C++ engine `cpp-wasm`, and the JavaScript build `java-js` comes last.
sec.teavm.p2: Static methods marked `@JSExport` become the exports of the compiled module ({src:teavm-web/src/main/java/sternhalma/web/Web.java}). In both builds, the TypeScript code calls them directly, as ordinary JavaScript functions, and gets the result as the return value. The JavaScript build is an ES module whose exports are plain functions. The Wasm GC build is loaded with `TeaVM.wasmGC.load(url)`, and the `exports` of the instance are exported WebAssembly functions, which are real JavaScript functions as well. TeaVM maps the types at this boundary: primitives other than `long` become numbers, `long` becomes `BigInt`, a `String` becomes a JavaScript string, and primitive arrays become typed arrays.
sec.teavm.p3: The builds differ in what lies behind the call. In the JavaScript build, the Java objects live on the JavaScript heap. In the Wasm GC build, they live in the browser's garbage-collected heap but stay opaque to JavaScript, which can only call exported functions. TeaVM copies arrays across the boundary by default. The annotation `@JSByRef` passes an array without a copy, but the Wasm GC backend does not support it, so the project marks the table parameter `@JSByRef(optional = true)`, which falls back to the copy. Apart from the table, the facade of the classical engine (`Web`) passes only strings: the history goes in as one comma-separated string, and every method returns `ok …` or `error …` and never throws, because a Java exception would reach the page as an opaque object.
sec.teavm.p4: For comparison, the C++ engine, compiled with {term:emscripten|Emscripten}, passes only numbers: integers, floats and pointers. A pointer is an offset into the module's {term:linear-memory|linear memory}, one `ArrayBuffer` that can grow. To hand over the table, the TypeScript code reserves memory in the module, copies the bytes in, and passes pointer and length. Messages, copied data and running in the background are not properties of WebAssembly. In this project they come from the {term:web-worker|Web Worker} around each engine, for all three builds. The call into the engine module is a direct, synchronous function call. The figure follows one move request across both boundaries.
sec.teavm.p5: Measured in Node.js on an Apple M3 Max, without a worker, the Wasm GC build searched about {n:0.96} million nodes per second, about {n:0.69} times the JVM. The C++ WebAssembly build was about {n:1.95} times as fast as the Wasm GC build, and the JavaScript build reached about {n:0.26} million nodes per second ({src:docs/web-benchmark.md}). Other jobs ran on the machine during that run. The shipped Wasm GC files have {n:609221} bytes, {n:208705} with gzip ({src:docs/web-ui.md}).
sec.teavm.p6: The network engines split the work. TeaVM compiles the Java search without the {term:forward-pass|forward pass}; the forward pass runs in C++ WebAssembly or in WebGPU. The reason is a measurement on an Apple M3 Max at batch 1: the scalar Java network compiled by TeaVM reached only 126 to 163 positions per second, the C++ WebAssembly backend about {n:3100} with SIMD and about {n:4000} with relaxed SIMD ({src:docs/web-ui.md}). The browser build has no Vector API path.
sec.worker.title: The Web Worker boundary
sec.worker.p1: Every browser engine runs in a module {term:web-worker|Web Worker}: the two Java builds, the C++ engine and the network engines ({src:web/src/engines/java/index.ts}). This is a design choice of the project. A worker is a second thread with no access to the page's objects or to the DOM. The page reaches it only through {term:post-message|postMessage}, and the browser copies each message with the {term:structured-clone|structured clone} algorithm; a buffer that the sender lists for transfer is moved instead (see below). The main thread never runs a search, so the board stays responsive while the engine thinks.
sec.worker.p2: The protocol is one request, one reply ({src:web/src/engines/protocol.ts}). Each request carries an `id` and a type such as `init`, `newGame`, `legalMoves` or `choose`. The worker handles one request after the other, in arrival order, and answers with `{id, ok, result}` or with an error code. The client keeps a table of open requests by id and resolves the matching {term:promise|Promise} when the reply arrives. Progress events carry the id of the running request.
sec.worker.p3: The page sends the table file to a new worker as a {term:transferable|transferred} `ArrayBuffer`. The browser moves such a buffer instead of copying it, and the sender loses it. The page therefore keeps the original and transfers a copy to each new worker ({src:web/src/engines/client.ts}). Because the search runs inside one synchronous call, nothing can interrupt it from outside. Cancel therefore terminates the worker, starts a new one, sends `init` with the kept table, and replays the game.
sec.worker.p4: The workers share no memory with the page. A `SharedArrayBuffer` would need {term:cross-origin-isolation|cross-origin isolation}, and that needs two HTTP headers that GitHub Pages cannot send. The C++ build therefore uses no threads and no `SharedArrayBuffer` ({src:cpp/CMakeLists.txt}). The network engines cross the call boundary once per batch of 1 to {n:4096} positions, not once per position: the Java search collects the positions, the C++ or WebGPU forward pass evaluates them in one call, and the search continues ({src:web/src/engines/net/core.ts}). The same batching idea decides the speed on the GPU ({sec:java/tornadovm|GPU kernels with TornadoVM}).

fig.hilla.title: One call from the page to Java and back
fig.hilla.wire.title: The data at this step
fig.hilla.wire.idle: Step through the call. This card shows the data at each step: where they are and in which form.
fig.hilla.steplist: Steps of the call, in order
fig.hilla.caption: The function GameEndpoint.choose looks local, but each call is one HTTP POST with the arguments as JSON. The page gets a copy of the result; the Java record stays on the server. The static build of this site has no such path.
fig.hilla.narr.idle: Two lanes, browser and server, with the network between them. Six parts take part in one call. Step forward to follow it.
fig.hilla.narr.build: Before any call, at build time: Hilla reads GameEndpoint.java and writes GameEndpoint.ts with the same method names.
fig.hilla.narr.call: The page calls choose like a local async function and gets a Promise. The Java method is out of reach: it runs in another process.
fig.hilla.narr.pack: The generated function hands name and arguments to ConnectClient. It turns them into JSON text and builds a POST with the CSRF token.
fig.hilla.narr.wire: The request crosses the network. Only text travels: no object and no reference.
fig.hilla.narr.unpack: Hilla checks the token and the access rule, turns the JSON into Java values (String, int[], int) and calls the method of the bean.
fig.hilla.narr.run: The Java method runs on the JVM: it replays the history, waits for a free slot and searches. The page keeps waiting on the Promise.
fig.hilla.narr.reply: The record ServerChoice becomes JSON text and travels back.
fig.hilla.narr.resolve: The client parses the JSON, and the Promise resolves with a plain object. It is a copy: the Java record stays on the server.

fig.hilla.step.reply: Engines.java back to ConnectClient, as JSON

fig.boundary.title: One call of choose() across two boundaries
fig.boundary.variant.label: Engine build
fig.boundary.caption: Messages, copies and the background thread come from the Web Worker and hold for all three builds. Inside the worker, the TypeScript wrapper calls the engine directly and waits for the return. The builds differ in what may cross that call. Shown: the classical browser engine. The counts are read from the source code, not measured.
fig.boundary.narr.idle: Two boundaries. The page reaches the worker only through messages. Inside the worker, TypeScript calls the engine as a function. The switch changes only this inner boundary.
fig.boundary.narr.post: The page calls choose() and gets a promise at once. The request carries an id and travels as a message; the browser copies it (structured clone).
fig.boundary.narr.queue: The worker takes one request after the other. Its handler calls the TypeScript wrapper of the engine. Nothing crosses a boundary here.
fig.boundary.narr.call.js: A normal function call to an export of an ES module. Six strings go in; the history is one string of move numbers with commas. Same heap.
fig.boundary.narr.call.wasmgc: The same call, now to an exported WebAssembly function. TeaVM converts the six strings into Java strings. Java objects never leave the module.
fig.boundary.narr.call.cpp: Only numbers can cross. The wrapper replays the game: one call to start, one call per move (N calls; N is the number of moves played so far), two calls to read the side to move and a counter, then the search call.
fig.boundary.narr.run: The search runs inside the call, and the call returns only when the search is done. The worker thread is busy and cannot read its next message. The page stays free. Cancel can only terminate the worker.
fig.boundary.narr.return.teavm: One string comes back: “ok” and seven fields. The wrapper splits it into numbers. An error is a string too; no Java exception crosses.
fig.boundary.narr.return.cpp: The move is the return value, one integer. Six more calls fetch score, depth, node count and flags. In total N + 10 calls, with N the number of moves played so far.
fig.boundary.narr.reply: The worker posts the result with the id of the request, and the browser copies it again. The page finds the promise by the id and resolves it. Two messages in total.
fig.boundary.lanes.aria: Path of the call from the page to the engine and back
fig.boundary.lane.page.note: holds the promise and the open requests
fig.boundary.lane.glue.note: request in, engine calls out, result back
fig.boundary.lane.engine.mem.js: JS heap, shared with the wrapper
fig.boundary.lane.engine.mem.wasmgc: Wasm GC heap, closed to JavaScript
fig.boundary.lane.engine.mem.cpp: linear memory: one block of bytes
fig.boundary.wall.msg.tag: messages only, each one a copy
fig.boundary.pay.label: What crosses at this step
fig.boundary.pay.note.idle: Step forward to follow the call.
fig.boundary.cmp.caption: The call boundary of the three builds
fig.boundary.cell.call.js: An export of the generated ES module: a plain JavaScript function.
fig.boundary.cell.call.wasmgc: An export of the loaded WebAssembly instance: also a JS function.
fig.boundary.cell.call.cpp: An exported C function; its name starts with an underscore.
fig.boundary.cell.types.js: TeaVM maps Java types to these; long becomes BigInt. This project passes strings.
fig.boundary.cell.types.wasmgc: The same mapping. A Java object stays opaque to JavaScript.
fig.boundary.cell.types.cpp: Nothing else. A string or an array is a pointer to bytes in the module's memory.
fig.boundary.cell.bulk.js: TeaVM copies arrays by default. With @JSByRef, the table passes without a copy.
fig.boundary.cell.bulk.wasmgc: TeaVM copies arrays. The Wasm GC backend does not support @JSByRef; “optional = true” falls back to the copy.
fig.boundary.cell.bulk.cpp: The wrapper copies by hand: reserve memory in the module, copy the bytes in, call with pointer and length, release.
fig.boundary.cell.memory.js: The JS heap, shared with the wrapper.
fig.boundary.cell.memory.wasmgc: Objects of the module in the browser's garbage-collected heap; closed to JavaScript.
fig.boundary.cell.memory.cpp: One ArrayBuffer that can grow; after it grows, old views on it are invalid.
fig.boundary.cell.thread.all: The same for all three: in the Web Worker, on the thread of the caller. The call returns when the work is done.
fig.boundary.also.head: Also true at these boundaries
fig.boundary.also.transfer: At start, the page sends the table file (rows2.bin) as a transferred buffer: moved, not copied. The sender loses it, so the page transfers a copy and keeps the original for a restart.
fig.boundary.also.cancel: A running search cannot be interrupted from outside. Cancel terminates the worker and starts a new one.
fig.boundary.also.batch: The network engines cross the call boundary once per batch of 1 to 4,096 positions, not once per position. The figure "What one GPU call costs" in High-speed Java shows why batches matter.
